specPoints.text: describe the red-shift in light received from galaxies at different distances away from the Earth
explain why the red-shift of galaxies provides evidence for the expansion of the universe

primer.text: The Doppler effect works on light too: a receding source's wavelengths stretch towards the red end (redshift), an approaching one's squeeze towards the blue (blueshift). Distant galaxies show bigger redshifts than nearby ones — the further the galaxy, the faster it flees — and that pattern is the expansion of the universe written in light.

lessons.title: Redshift and blueshift
lessons.opening: Light obeys the Doppler effect like every other wave. When a source moves away, its light's wavelength increases towards the red end of the spectrum — redshift — and its frequency falls; when it approaches, the wavelength shortens towards blue — blueshift — and the frequency rises.
keyPoints: When a light source moves away, its wavelength increases — redshift.
When a light source approaches, its wavelength decreases — blueshift.
An increase in wavelength is a decrease in frequency, and the reverse.
In visible light, red carries the longest wavelength and the smallest frequency.
The motorbike pitch analogy: receding sound drops in frequency, exactly like redshifted light.

low.restatement: Away = stretched = redder = lower frequency; towards = squeezed = bluer = higher frequency.
low.analogy: Duck ripples again, but in light: the bow-wave bunches blue, the wake trails red.
low.examPointer: In the visible spectrum, red = longest wavelength and lowest frequency — quote the pair.

medium.restatement: One wave law does the work: fixed light speed forces the wavelength-frequency trade.
medium.analogy: A fixed-budget shopping trip: if each item (wavelength) costs more, fewer items (cycles per second) fit.
medium.examPointer: Tie the motorbike-pitch analogy to light explicitly when explaining.

options.text: receding sources lowering frequency, as redshift does for light

check.modelAnswer: Redshift: the stretching of a light wave's wavelength as its source recedes from the observer.

check.stem: State the wavelength and frequency changes for blueshift.
check.modelAnswer: Blueshift shortens the wavelength and raises the frequency as the source approaches.

check.stem: Explain why redshifted light has a lower frequency.
check.modelAnswer: Light travels at a fixed speed, so wavelength and frequency trade against each other; a stretched wavelength must come with a reduced frequency.

check.stem: A star's spectral lines sit at shorter wavelengths than the reference. State the star's motion.
check.modelAnswer: Shorter wavelengths mean blueshift, so the star is moving towards the observer.

lessons.title: Redshift and the expanding universe
sourceHeadings: Redshift diagram for a light spectrum
lessons.opening: Comparing the Sun's spectrum with a distant galaxy's shows the galaxy's spectral lines shifted towards red: the expansion of the universe stretches the light waves as they travel. Distant galaxies redshift more than nearby ones, so the greater the distance, the faster the galaxy flees — evidence that the universe is expanding and supports the Big Bang.
keyPoints: Spectral lines from distant galaxies are shifted towards the red end of the spectrum.
The expansion of the universe stretches light waves, increasing their wavelength.
Distant galaxies show more redshift than nearby galaxies.
Greater distance goes with greater redshift — the most distant galaxies flee fastest.
This redshift-distance pattern supports the Big Bang theory and the expanding universe.

low.restatement: Distant lines shifted red → galaxies receding → further means faster → expanding universe.
low.analogy: Ambulance siren for light: the whole sky's ambulances are driving away, and the far ones are speeding most.
low.examPointer: Chain the logic: redshift → recession → distance-speed pattern → expansion → Big Bang support.

medium.restatement: Expansion stretches light in flight, so the spectrum itself is the expansion's ruler.
medium.analogy: A tape measure being stretched while you read it: the markings (spectral lines) slide apart as the tape (space) lengthens.
medium.examPointer: Say the wavelengths increase because the universe's expansion stretches the light waves.

check.stem: State what redshift provides evidence for.
check.modelAnswer: Redshift provides evidence that the universe is expanding and supports the Big Bang theory.

check.stem: State the relationship between a galaxy's distance and its speed away from us.
check.modelAnswer: The further away the galaxy, the faster it moves away from the Earth.

check.stem: Explain why redshift supports the idea of an expanding universe.
check.modelAnswer: The spectral lines of distant galaxies are stretched towards red because the universe's expansion stretches the light waves, showing the galaxies are moving away — and the more distant the galaxy, the greater the shift and the faster the retreat.

check.stem: Galaxy P shows a small redshift; galaxy Q, further away, shows a large one. Compare their speeds.
check.modelAnswer: Galaxy Q recedes faster: greater distance goes with greater redshift and therefore a greater speed away from Earth.

glossary.definition: The increase in observed wavelength when a light source moves away from the observer.
The decrease in observed wavelength when a light source approaches the observer.
The dark or bright lines in a spectrum whose displacement reveals redshift.
